Quick reasoning and next step:
1. Money and benefits: keep the job if you need steady pay, health insurance, or to keep your resume gap-free. If you can cover 2–6 months of expenses and you’re prepared for a gap, quitting is workable.
2. Safety and mental health: if the yelling is harassment, threats, or causing severe stress/health problems, leaving sooner is reasonable — document incidents and get advice from HR or a lawyer if needed.

Short answer: Maybe — it depends on your role, industry, level, location, and career goal. Tell me one thing and I’ll be specific: what’s your current title and the next job you want? Sensible default: you’re a mid‑level project manager in tech aiming for senior PM or program manager.
Quick checklist — when PMP is worth it
1) Role match: Hiring managers or job postings for your target role list “PMP” or “project management certification” often — PMP helps.
2) Experience level: You need 3–5 years’ documented project experience to qualify for the exam; it’s most useful once you have that experience.
3) Career path: If you want to move into program, portfolio, PMO, or government/defense work, PMP is highly valuable. In product/tech roles it’s less decisive unless employers require it.
4) Industry & geography: Consulting, construction, engineering, and government value PMP strongly; many US employers give pay/advancement bumps for PMP. In some European and startup tech markets, other certifications (Prince2, Agile/Scrum) or demonstrable outcomes matter more.
5) Time & cost: Expect 3–6 months study, $555 exam fee (non‑member) or $405 (PMI member), plus prep course/books/practice exams. Consider ROI vs time to get experience or other credentials (CSM, SAFe, data/tech certs).
6) Alternatives: If your hiring market prizes Agile, a Certified ScrumMaster/Product Owner or practical portfolio (delivered products, metrics) can be faster, cheaper, and more relevant.
7) Employer support: If your employer will pay or counts it toward promotion, that strongly tips toward doing it.

How I’d decide for you (one next step)
- If you confirm your current title and target role (or say “use the default”), I’ll tell you: odds it helps, likely pay bump, whether to pick PMP or something else, and a 90‑day plan to get it (or to skip it and use an alternative). Which do you want me to use: tell your title and target, or use the sensible default?

replies:
Short answer: usually yes — but not always.

Playback: You said "I'm on an F-1 visa." Is that right?

Why: F-1 is a student visa. Immediately after graduation you can work on Optional Practical Training (OPT) for up to 12 months (or up to 36 months if you qualify for the STEM extension). OPT does not require employer sponsorship. But OPT is temporary and employer sponsorship will be needed if you want to continue working after your OPT/OPT STEM expires.
When an employer must sponsor:
- If you want a full-time work authorization beyond your OPT/OPT STEM period, the employer must sponsor an H-1B (or another work visa/status). H-1B sponsorship is common for F-1 grads; other employer-sponsored routes exist but are less common.
Timing and practical points:
- H-1B cap-subject employers file petitions in early April for an October 1 start (regular cap). You generally need employer agreement to file.
- Cap-exempt employers (some universities, non-profits affiliated with universities, government research organizations) can hire without the April lottery constraints.
- If you’re on OPT when an employer files an H-1B and it’s selected, you may get cap-gap extension of your work authorization to bridge to H-1B start date.
- STEM 24-month extension increases your time to work without sponsorship and improves chances to remain employed while a sponsor files H-1B.
What to tell employers when applying:
- Be transparent: list your current status (F-1, on OPT or seeking OPT start date) and whether you will need H-1B sponsorship after OPT (yes). Employers prefer to know whether you need sponsorship now or later.
- If you will be on OPT through the job start and need sponsorship only after (or you’re eligible for STEM extension), state that.
If you want, I can:
- Add "Needs visa sponsorship after OPT" as a standing instruction to your account (it will save your exact words). Default phrasing I’ll use: "Needs H‑1B sponsorship after OPT/STEM OPT ends." Ask one short question and I'll save it.
- Or answer a specific scenario: e.g., you graduate in May, need a job starting June, eligible for STEM? If you tell me your graduation month and whether your degree is on the STEM list (or I can default to "not STEM"), I’ll say the practical timeline and what to tell employers.
